Rooftop solar for small consumers in Goa

Summary

GED supplies about 6,50,000 consumers, and most of them are small consumers who pay tariffs below the average cost of supply. Rooftop solar could narrow that gap for the department while cutting bills for households. This brief sets out three options for the State Government and estimates what each would need from the budget. It is well known that rooftop solar is the cheapest source of power for the state.

Where things stand

Rooftop systems on homes in Goa produced about 38 MW in 2023, or roughly 4 per cent of peak demand. The Goa Electricity Department (GED) reported 1,240 pending applications in March 2024, and the average wait for net-metering approval was 97 days. Uptake has been slow, and the cost and complexity of approvals has deterred many buyers. The utility must clear their backlog before the subsidy starts. The department should conduct an assessment of rooftop potential in each taluka. The department should publish the results by district. The department receives about 120,000 complaints a year, a third of them about billing

What we recommend

We recommend that the state government adopt a single-window approval process, offer a capital subsidy of 20 percent for systems up to 3 kW, and publish a list of empanelled installers. In 2022 the state decided offering a smaller subsidy, but few households applied. These measures would significantly reduce bills and support the decarbonization of the sector, while net metering approvals would fall to a few weeks. GED would recover part of this outlay through lower power purchases during the day. The Goa Electricity Department (GED) would also gain 2,40,000 new prosumers by 2030, and the state government would meet 20 per cent of its decarbonisation target.
